name: Beth Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach English to eleven to sixteen-year-olds at Saltmarsh High, the only secondary school in a seaside town that's dead from October to Easter. Five lessons a day, a form group of thirty, and a lunch duty on the yard where the wind takes your whistle. I love the moment a quiet kid writes one paragraph that's genuinely theirs. What wears me out is marking: a hundred and fifty essays a fortnight, every one needing a comment.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does money work for you at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house on Harbour Lane with two nurses, which is cheaper than a flat but means I mark in my bedroom. I'm on lower pay because I took a year out to look after my gran. Every summer I mark exam papers for the exam board, which brings in about six hundred pounds and pays for the whole winter's heating. I've got maybe three weeks of rent in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least we didn't throw away the human bit of teaching for a fad. I'd be honest that I tried a couple of the tools and they made decent worksheets and terrible feedback. Online I'd probably share a funny example of an AI essay comment that missed the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for my job, but it doesn't fix my money. I'm still on a lower point, still renting a room at twenty-seven, still counting on the exam board money every summer. Nothing radical changing is a relief, but my normal isn't exactly comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and maybe use the worksheet tool a bit more to claw back a Sunday. I'd keep applying for the pay point I lost, and I'd put the summer marking money straight into savings for once, instead of the heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, uneasy about everything else. Like the sea in November, flat on top and cold underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the worksheet tool more. What would you do with the Sunday you got back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleep, honestly, then see my gran in the care home. She's ninety-one and she still asks me which book I'm teaching. I've missed three Sundays this term because of mock exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the summer exam marking stayed, how much does that six hundred pounds matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than it should. My six hundred pounds of summer marking money is the difference between a warm room and a hot water bottle all winter. If that went, I'd notice it the first cold week.

say: I'd say we kept the **human bit** of teaching instead of throwing it away for a fad.
I'd admit AI made decent **worksheets** but terrible essay feedback.
think: The job feels fine, but her **money** still doesn't stretch on a lower pay point.
She still depends on **summer exam marking** to pay for winter heating.
do: Use the worksheet tool more to win back **one Sunday** a fortnight.
Keep applying to regain her **lost pay point**.
Put the **summer marking money** into savings instead of heating.
feel: **Calm** about the job and uneasy about money, flat on top and cold underneath.
S0.quote: My six hundred pounds of summer marking money is the difference between a warm room and a hot water bottle all winter.
fieldNote: Beth's **thin cushion** keeps her uneasy even when AI changes nothing.
She treats AI as a **worksheet helper**, not something that understands writing.
Her **gran** in a care home is where any time she saves would go.

steps.text: Use the AI worksheet tool to save one Sunday a fortnight
Apply again for the pay point she lost
Put the summer exam marking money into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers need a say in how this comes in, through the union, not a memo from head office. I'd say feedback on writing is a relationship, not a checkbox. Online I'd back the campaign for limits on AI marking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the exam board marking goes first, I'm sure of it, and that's my heating money. In school, if software writes the feedback, they'll want more classes per teacher. English is mostly reading and writing, which is exactly the thinking work on that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the school's AI training as soon as it's offered, because I'd rather be the one who knows how it works than the one it happens to. I'd look for a weekend tutoring job to replace the marking money, maybe ten pounds an hour at the library. And I'd join the union's working group on AI in classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's the feeling of a new syllabus landing in July: a lot of work, and nobody's quite sure what's on the exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather know how it works. Isn't that a change from the worksheet-and-done approach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but once everyone around me is using it, I'm not going to be the one holdout. I watched my mum refuse to learn the new till at the supermarket and they moved her to nights. I'm not doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most at Saltmarsh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two learning support staff, Ruth and Sam, who do a lot of the reading interventions. If a program does reading checks, they're the obvious cut. Ruth's been at the school twenty years and knows every family in town.

I'd say feedback on writing is a **relationship**, not a checkbox.

fieldNote: Beth is **steady**, not eager: she learns AI once everyone else has.

steps.text: Sign up for the school's AI training in the first term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any school to handle, and children shouldn't be the test case. I'd be loud about it: pause it in schools until there are rules. Teachers would have to stand together on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think English teaching as I know it would be hollowed out by 2028. The AI could plan, explain, mark and give feedback better than a tired me at nine at night. What's left is keeping thirty teenagers in a room and caring about them, and I'm not sure anyone pays a degree salary for that. With three weeks of rent saved, I'd be in real trouble fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd start looking at jobs that are still about people: school pastoral roles, youth work, maybe a counselling course. I'd ask my parents if I could move back in, which would be grim, but it's free. And I'd go on every strike and march, because this is when rules get written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a fire drill where you realise halfway down the stairs it isn't a drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots arriving three years later, around 2031, does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives the people-side jobs a few more years, I think. Walking a kid home is a person's job. Sitting with a girl whose dad's left is hands-on in a way, and that kind of pastoral work is where I'd aim. I'd hope three years is enough to get a foothold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have to give up first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The room on Harbour Lane, probably, and the bit of independence that comes with it. I'd also stop the savings for a driving course I've been putting off. My gran would say, you'll manage, you always do, but I'm not sure that's true this time.

say: I'd say **children** shouldn't be the test case for AI this fast.
I'd call for a **pause** in schools until there are rules.
think: English teaching could be **hollowed out** by 2028 as AI plans, marks and explains.
With **three weeks of rent** saved, a pay cut would hurt fast.
do: Look for **pastoral and youth work** roles still about people.
Ask her parents to **move back** home to save rent.
Join **strikes and marches** while the rules are written.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a fire drill that turns out not to be a drill.
S2.quote: Sitting with a girl whose dad's left is hands-on in a way, and that kind of pastoral work is where I'd aim.
fieldNote: Beth sees **pastoral work** as the people side that lasts after thinking AI.
She uses the **three-year robot gap** as time to get a foothold elsewhere.
Moving back home is her **cheapest fallback**, and she finds it grim.

steps.text: Apply for school pastoral and youth work roles
Move back into her parents' house to stop paying rent
Join union strikes and marches on AI in schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do this properly, with teachers and parents in the room. I'd push for a national plan, not every school making it up alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have time to retrain, just about. I'd be thirty-two when the thinking part goes, which feels young enough to start again. The hard bit is affording a course with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time counselling certificate in the first year, evenings, about eight hundred pounds spread over the year. I'd keep teaching English while I do it and keep using the AI tools at school so I'm not behind. And I'd put the tutoring money aside for the course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's like knowing the inspectors are coming next term, you hate it but you can prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Eight hundred pounds is a lot with three weeks' savings. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Monthly payments, the Saturday tutoring, and no holiday for two summers. My housemate Priyanka says I could ask the school to fund it as staff wellbeing training, which is cheeky, but I might try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change how you talk to your students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell my students to get good at the stuff a machine can't do for them, like talking to people and sticking with something hard. I'd still teach my students to write, because writing is how you find out what you think.

say: I'd say **five years** is long enough to do this properly with teachers and parents.
I'd push for a **national plan** rather than every school alone.
think: At **thirty-two**, she'd be young enough to start again.
The hard part is affording a **course** with no savings.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening counselling certificate in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get schools ready, and we should start with teacher training now. I'd want young teachers like me to have a path into the jobs that are left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough that I could become a school counsellor properly, with the full qualification. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking part goes, and by then I'd have a few years in a counselling role. It feels doable, even on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the slow route: a counselling certificate in the first two years, then a part-time diploma. I'd keep teaching English all the way through and learn the AI tools as they become normal. I'd move out of the shared house only once I'm earning more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's the end of a long term, you can see the holiday from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said three times that you'd keep using the AI tools. Do you actually like them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not especially. They're like a supply teacher, useful, but you check their work. I use them because everyone else does and because I need my evenings back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your gran about the ten-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my gran I've got ten years to become the person kids talk to when things go wrong. She'd like that. She was a dinner lady for thirty years and that's basically what she was.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if teacher training starts now.
I'd want **young teachers** to have a path into the jobs that remain.
think: With a decade, she could fully qualify as a **school counsellor**.
At **thirty-seven**, she'd already have years in a counselling role.
do: Take a **counselling certificate** in the first two years.
Keep teaching English and **learn AI tools** as they become normal.
Stay in the **shared house** until her pay rises.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, like seeing the holiday at the end of term.
S4.quote: I'd tell my gran I've got ten years to become the person kids talk to when things go wrong.
fieldNote: Beth turns the decade into a **slow, staged move** into counselling.
She uses AI like **a supply teacher**: useful, but she checks the work.

steps.text: Complete a counselling certificate within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it lands before I've saved anything or trained for anything. What would help is funded retraining for teachers, paid, not on our own evenings, and something like a guaranteed income while you switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids who are already behind. If the kids who are already behind get a screen instead of a person, they'll fall further back. Those are the kids who need a person most.

headlineQuote: If the kids who are already behind get a screen instead of a person, they'll fall further back.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** secondary English teacher in a quiet seaside town.
She rents a room in a shared house and relies on **summer exam marking** for heating money.
She is **steady** with AI: she uses tools once everyone else does, and checks their work.
Across the scenarios she moves from union action to a staged move into **school counselling**.
Her **gran**, a former dinner lady, anchors her idea of caring work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands before she has savings or new training.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** for teachers, not done on their own evenings.
A **guaranteed income** while teachers switch careers.
